notes.text: Rulers, and elders, and scribes — Who were eminent for power, for wisdom, and for learning.
Annas, who had been the high priest, and Caiaphas, who was so then.
By what name — By what authority, have ye done this? - They seem to speak ambiguously on purpose.
Then Peter, filled with the Holy Ghost — That moment. God moves his instruments, not when they please, but just when he sees it needful. Ye rulers - He gives them the honour due to their office.

Be it known to you all — Probably the herald of God proclaimed this with a loud voice. Whom God hath raised from the dead - They knew in their own consciences that it was so. And though they had hired the soldiers to tell a most senseless and incredible tale to the contrary, Matt. xxviii, 12, 15, yet it is observable, they did not, so far as we can learn, dare to plead it before Peter and John.
Psalm cxviii, 22.

There is no other name whereby we must be saved — The apostle uses a beautiful gradation, from the temporal deliverance which had been wrought for the poor cripple, by the power of Christ, to that of a much nobler and more important kind, which is wrought by Christ for impotent and sinful souls. He therein follows the admirable custom of his great Lord and Master, who continually took occasion from earthly to speak of spiritual things.

glossa.text:
*This is the stone. ((RAB.))* Here, answering the things asked of him, he preaches concerning Christ, and most of all concerning David, in whom, as in their own patriarch, they believed before all others.

*Rejected. ((AUG.))* Of the rejected stone no history is had.

notes.text: Lie down — To repose myself at noon, as the manner was in those hot countries. Green - Where there is both delight and plenty of provisions.
Restoreth — Hebrew. He bringeth it back; from its errors and wandering. For - Not for any worth in me, but for the glory of his justice, and faithfulness, and goodness.
Thy rod and thy staff — Two words denoting the same thing, and both designing God's pastoral care over him.

A table — Thou furnishest me with plenty of provisions and comforts. Oil - With aromatic ointments, which were then used at great feasts; thy comforts delight my soul. Runneth over - Thou hast given me a plentiful portions, signified by the cup, given to the guests by the master of the feast. This psalm is generally thought to have been composed by David, upon bringing the ark of God from the house of Obed- edom, into the tabernacle which David had built for it, 2 Sam. vi, 12, 17. Wherein he hath a farther prospect to the temple, which he earnestly desired and intended to build. Moreover because the tabernacle, and temple, and ark, were types of Christ, and of his church and of heaven. David extended his thoughts to them also, or at least the Holy Ghost designed to comprehend them under these typical expressions. He shews God's sovereignty over the world, ver. 1, 2. Who shall receive his blessing, ver. 3-6. An exhortation to receive Christ, ver. 7-10. A psalm of David.

glossa.text: *A psalm of David.* ((CASS.)) The Prophet foretold the return of the people from Babylon. *The Lord ruleth me.* A psalm of mercy, enumerating ten graces, that all may hope in the mercy of God. ((AUG.)) The Church speaks of Christ.

*In a place of pasture.* ((CASS.)) The first grace, a place of pasture, that is, the divine word, which fattens those who meditate upon it. *Upon the water.* The second grace, the water of refreshment.

*My soul.* ((ID.)) The third grace, etc., *as far as* but first he brought me up upon the water of refreshment, first he converted my soul. *He hath led.* ((ID.)) The fourth, in that he led me upon the precepts of charity. *Upon the paths.* ((AUG.)) The narrower commandments and the more perfect counsels; as it were upon paths few just men walk, even as paths are narrower than roads.

*For though I shall walk.* ((CASS.)) The fifth, that in the shadow of death he fears no evils. *Thou art with me.* ((AUG.)) In the heart by faith, that after the shadow of death I may be with thee. *Thy rod.* ((CASS.)) The sixth, correction; or the rod is strictness, which converts vices. The staff is governance, which upholds the faithful.

*Thou hast prepared in my sight.* ((CASS.)) The seventh, the table of the Lord, the blessed banqueting, the fullness of faith, the heavenly food, of which the Apostle: *He that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh judgment to himself. In my sight a table:* even if not that of the wicked. Of this it is said: *But these at the table of the rich man,* that is, of Christ, *know that thou too must prepare the like,* that is, to suffer as he did. *Thou hast anointed:* the eighth, the anointing of the head, namely of Christ, which was dried up by no barrenness of sin, whence the rest of the members rejoice, because from the head the ointment ran down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, and unto the skirt of his garment. *And my chalice.* The ninth, the chalice, the blood of Christ, which so inebriates that it makes men sober. *Mine,* because I receive it. Or, thine, because thou givest it. The table and the chalice, flesh and blood, although they are one sacrament, yet under diverse species, because both are taken, are here set down separately.
*And mercy.* ((CASS.)) The tenth, mercy following after unto keeping, which goes before unto the conferring of grace.
*And that I may dwell.* ((HIER.)) This is joined to all the things above. As though: thou hast placed, thou hast brought up, thou hast led, etc., and this to the end that I may dwell.

notes.text: The word God is not in the original. It was omitted by the apostle just as the particular name is omitted by Mary, when she says to the gardener, "Sir, if thou hast born him hence;" and by the church, when she says, "Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth," So i, 2; in both which places there is a language, a very emphatical language, even in silence. It declares how totally the thoughts were possessed by the blessed and glorious subject. It expresses also the superlative dignity and amiableness of the person meant, as though He, and He alone, was, or deserved to be, both known and admired by all. Because he laid down his life — Not merely for sinners, but for us in particular. From this truth believed, from this blessing enjoyed, the love of our brethren takes its rise, which may very justly be admitted as an evidence that our faith is no delusion.

But whoso hath this world's good — Worldly substance, far less valuable than life. And seeth his brother have need - The very sight of want knocks at the door of the spectator's heart. And shutteth up - Whether asked or not. His bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him - Certainly not at all, however he may talk, 1 John iii, 18, of loving God.
Not in word — Only. But in deed - In action: not in tongue by empty professions, but in truth.

And hereby we know — We have a further proof by this real, operative love. That we are of the truth - That we have true faith, that we are true children of God. And shall assure our hearts before him - Shall enjoy the assurance of his favour, and the "testimony of a good conscience toward God." The heart, in St. John's language, is the conscience. The word conscience is not found in his writings.

For if we have not this testimony, if in anything our heart, our own conscience, condemn us, much more does God, who is greater than our heart — An infinitely holier and a more impartial Judge. And knoweth all things - So that there is no hope of hiding it from him.

If our heart condemn us not — If our conscience, duly enlightened by the word and Spirit of God, and comparing all our thoughts, words, and works with that word, pronounce that they agree therewith. Then have we confidence toward God - Not only our consciousness of his favour continues and increases, but we have a full persuasion, that whatsoever we ask we shall receive of him.

And this is his commandment — All his commandments in one word. That we should believe and love - in the manner and degree which he hath taught. This is the greatest and most important command that ever issued from the throne of glory. If this be neglected, no other can be kept: if this be observed, all others are easy.

And he that keepeth his commandments — That thus believes and loves. Abideth in him, and God in him: and hereby we know that he abideth in us, by the Spirit which he hath given us - Which witnesses with our spirits that we are his children, and brings forth his fruits of peace, love, holiness. This is the transition to the treating of the Holy Spirit which immediately follows.

glossa.text: *In this we know,* etc. Many reasons having been set forth concerning the charity that is to be had, at length he subjoins concerning the perfection of charity, under the example of the Lord's passion. Peter is admonished to have this, when to the Lord questioning him he professed that he loved him, to whom it is said: *But when thou shalt be old, thou shalt stretch forth thy hands, and another shall gird thee, and lead thee whither thou wouldest not ((Joan. XXI))*. In which words he was taught to lay down his life for the sheep. *For no man hath greater charity than that a man lay down his life for his friends ((Ibid. XV))*.

*He that shall have,* etc. If, whether from the opportunity of the time or from human infirmity, it has not befallen us to lay down our lives, we ought at least to lay down our goods for the brethren, and this is the nourishment of charity. He who has learned to give his own property will one day be able to lay down himself.

*Little children, let us not love,* etc. Because charity is not perfect in him; who does not lay down his life for the brethren, or who at least does not give money. Therefore, that you may have perfect charity, *little children* of the same father. *Let us not love in word, neither in tongue.* By word is understood pure speech, not work; by tongue, manifold discourse, as some wish by often-repeated speeches to commend their affection. *But in deed.* Because even if we are deceived in our love out of human infirmity, we are not deceived in the reward, because God is greater than our heart, and knows with what zeal all things are done. *And in truth.* If we bestow benefits with a simple intention, not for the sake of boasting, nor for the sake of any temporal advantage, but with regard to God alone.

*In this we know,* etc. In this, that we love the truth, we know that we are of the truth, that is, we know that we have this true love from God (who is truth), and from this love we know that we are in his sight, that is, that we deserve his sight, and in this also we persuade our hearts to devise better works. *And in the sight,* etc. That is, we persuade our hearts to have such thoughts as are worthy of the divine sight. For all who set themselves to do anything persuade their hearts to turn to meditating upon that same deed. But he who thinks evil things would hide them from God, if he could: but they who think good things most easily persuade their hearts to desire to be laid open to the sight of God, which is a sign of great perfection, when one's own work or thought rejoices to be seen by God.

*Because if it shall reprove.* And this is a great thing, that through love we have thoughts so clean that we wish to show them to God: because even if the conscience should accuse us within and should wish to lie hid from God, because we were doing our good deeds not with a good mind, yet we could not hide them from God, because he is greater than our heart, and knows all things: love therefore avails, which commends us to him from whom we cannot lie hid.

*And whatsoever we shall ask.* A great promise, and one to be desired by the faithful. But *if anyone* is so perverse that he is not delighted by the heavenly promises, let him at least fear what wisdom on the contrary thunders terribly: *He that turneth away his ear that he may not hear the law, his prayer shall be an abomination ((Prov. XXVIII))*.
*And this is the commandment.* He puts the commandment first in the singular number, and subjoins two, because these cannot be separated.

notes.text: But the hireling — It is not the bare receiving hire, which denominates a man a hireling: (for the labourer is worthy of his hire; Jesus Christ himself being the Judge: yea, and the Lord hath ordained, that they who preach the Gospel, should live of the Gospel:) but the loving hire: the loving the hire more than the work: the working for the sake of the hire. He is a hireling, who would not work, were it not for the hire; to whom this is the great (if not only) motive of working. O God! If a man who works only for hire is such a wretch, a mere thief and a robber, what is he who continually takes the hire, and yet does not work at all? The wolf - signifies any enemy who, by force or fraud, attacks the Christian's faith, liberty, or life. So the wolf seizeth and scattereth the flock - He seizeth some, and scattereth the rest; the two ways of hurting the flock of Christ.
The hireling fleeth because he is a hireling — Because he loves the hire, not the sheep.
I know my sheep — With a tender regard and special care: and am known of mine - With a holy confidence and affection.

As the Father knoweth me, and I know the Father — With such a knowledge as implies an inexpressible union: and I lay down my life - Speaking of the present time. For his whole life was only a going unto death.

I have also other sheep — Which he foreknew; which are not of this fold - Not of the Jewish Church or nation, but Gentiles. I must bring them likewise - Into my Church, the general assembly of those whose names are written in heaven. And there shall be one flock - (Not one fold, a plain false print) no corrupt or divided flocks remaining. And one shepherd - Who laid down his life for the sheep, and will leave no hireling among them. The unity both of the flock and the shepherd shall be completed in its season. The shepherd shall bring all into one flock: and the whole flock shall hear the one shepherd.
I lay down my life that I may take it again — I cheerfully die to expiate the sins of men, to the end I may rise again for their justification.

I lay it down of myself — By my own free act and deed. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again - I have an original power and right of myself, both to lay it down as a ransom, and to take it again, after full satisfaction is made, for the sins of the whole world. This commission have I received of my Father - Which I readily execute. He chiefly spoke of the Father, before his suffering: of his own glory, after it. Our Lord's receiving this commission as mediator is not to be considered as the ground of his power to lay down and resume his life. For this he had in himself, as having an original right to dispose thereof, antecedent to the Father's commission. But this commission was the reason why he thus used his power in laying down his life. He did it in obedience to his Father.

glossa.text: *But the hireling,* etc. The hireling is he who seeks the things that are his own, not the things that are Christ's; who serves God not for God's sake, but for some wage; who is blameworthy, and is not a son, but is nevertheless necessary and to be borne with. But the thief is always to be guarded against. Yet the prelates who are sons are shepherds also, and nevertheless there is one shepherd, because they are all members of him whose the sheep properly are. *And the wolf snatcheth.* The wolf is either the violent man who lays waste bodily, or the devil who scatters spiritually; and he who seeks not the souls of the sheep but his own things does not go to meet him by resisting or by rebuking evils, which is to flee, because fear is the flight of the mind: he flees lest he lose what he loves; whence, giving the cause of his flight, he adds: *Because he is a hireling,* and loves not the sheep, but his own things. But shepherds are not said to flee if they give way to persecution and preserve themselves for the profit of the sheep, to whom, though absent in body, they are present in spirit.

*I am the shepherd.* After the fault of the counterfeit shepherd, he again sets forth the form of the true one. *I am the good shepherd, and I lay down my life for the sheep.* Which he alone did not do, save that all his own and he himself are one, because he could do this without them, they not without him, without whom they can do nothing.

*And I.* The Son through himself knows the Father, we through him, as elsewhere: *No man hath seen God at any time, unless the Only-begotten who is in the bosom of the Father, he shall have declared him ((Matth. XI))*. Likewise: *no man knoweth the Son but the Father, neither doth anyone know the Father but the Son, and he to whom the Son will reveal him ((Matth. XI; Luc. X))*. *And I lay down my life.* This is the proof of love toward the Father and toward the sheep. So too Peter, confessing his love a third time, is bidden to feed the sheep and to die for them. *For the sheep.* For the sheep of the house of Israel which had perished, to whom he was bodily sent, from whom those which are of the Gentiles are not unlike; whence he says:
*I must.* Although through his own, because in them he himself is. *And my voice.* He does not say "of mine," because in them he himself speaks.
*Because I,* etc. ((AUG.)) The Word, from which he took manhood, that is, flesh and soul, etc., *as far as* not by its own power, but by the power of the Godhead inhabiting the flesh, namely.

hymns.title: The Lord's my shepherd, I'll not want
The King of love my shepherd is
How firm a foundation, ye saints of the Lord

echoes.text: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.
echoes.note: Verse 11 directly quotes Ps 118:22 (LXX 117:22), 'the stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner,' applied to the crucified-and-raised Jesus and turned polemically on 'you, the builders' (the rulers). High Volume (near-verbatim citation), high Recurrence (the rejected-stone testimonium pervades early Christian usage), and strong Thematic Coherence (rejection-then-vindication mirrors crucifixion-resurrection).

echoes.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Yahweh, “Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.
echoes.note: The 'stone' Christology in v.11 draws on the broader OT stone complex; Isa 28:16's precious cornerstone laid in Zion frequently fuses with Ps 118:22 in early Christian testimonia. No direct citation here, but the cornerstone vocabulary and foundation-of-salvation logic (leading into v.12) cohere with Isaiah's tested stone.

echoes.text: Declare and present it. Yes, let them take counsel together. Who has shown this from ancient time? Who has declared it of old? Haven’t I, Yahweh? There is no other God besides me, a just God and a Savior; There is no one besides me. “Look to me, and be saved, all the ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other.
echoes.note: Verse 12, 'there is salvation in none other... no other name... by which we must be saved,' echoes Isaiah's exclusivist monotheism of salvation: 'there is no other God besides me, a righteous God and a Savior; there is none besides me... be saved, all the ends of the earth.' The 'none other / no other' salvation formula maps onto Isaiah's 'none besides me.'

echoes.text: It will happen that whoever will call on Yahweh’s name shall be saved; for in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be those who escape, as Yahweh has said, and among the remnant, those whom Yahweh calls.
echoes.note: Verse 12's stress that salvation comes only through 'the name' echoes Joel 2:32 (LXX 3:5), 'everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved' — the same name-and-salvation linkage Peter cited at Pentecost (Acts 2:21), now narrowed to the name of Jesus. Thematic coherence is strong; the recurrence in Acts strengthens the link.

echoes.text: You saw until a stone was cut out without hands, which struck the image on its feet that were of iron and clay, and broke them in pieces. Then was the iron, the clay, the brass, the silver, and the gold, broken in pieces together, and became like the chaff of the summer threshing floors; and the wind carried them away, so that no place was found for them: and the stone that struck the image became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth.
echoes.note: Daniel's stone, cut without hands, that shatters the kingdoms and fills the earth, belongs to the same messianic stone-testimonia cluster; the contrast between human builders' rejection and God's exaltation of the stone resonates faintly with Daniel's God-given stone overturning earthly powers. Contested, no verbal link.

echoes.text: I myself am Yahweh; and besides me there is no savior.
echoes.note: 'I, even I, am the LORD, and besides me there is no savior' reinforces the exclusive-salvation claim of v.12. A faint reinforcing echo within the same Isaianic monotheism-of-salvation field as Isa 45:21-22; included for maximal coverage.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.id: The City of David and Old City, on the spurs above the Kidron Valley, c. 50 km from the Mediterranean. Pre-Israelite Jebus; named here as the seat of Adoni-Zedek, leader of the southern coalition.

places.name: Nazareth
places.id: Modern en-Nasira / Nazareth in Lower Galilee, c. 30 km west of the Sea of Galilee. A village of perhaps 200-400 in the early first century, identified through continuous habitation, tomb evidence, and the third-century Caesarea inscription naming it as a priestly course settlement.

echoes.text: If a poor man, one of your brothers, is with you within any of your gates in your land which Yahweh your God gives you, you shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother; but you shall surely open your hand to him, and shall surely lend him sufficient for his need, which he lacks.
echoes.note: 'You shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother,' but open your hand to his need, directly underlies 'sees his brother in need, and closes his heart of compassion against him.' John's image of the closed heart inverts the command to open hand and heart. The 'brother in need' vocabulary is shared.

echoes.text: Isn’t it to distribute your bread to the hungry, and that you bring the poor who are cast out to your house? When you see the naked, that you cover him; and that you not hide yourself from your own flesh?
echoes.note: True fasting is to share bread with the hungry and not hide oneself from one's own flesh, the prophetic demand to meet a needy brother's wants. John's test of love by sharing 'the world's goods' echoes this concrete charity. The 'do not hide from' your kin matches the closed heart John condemns.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: The Servant 'poured out his soul/life unto death' and bore the sin of many, the OT ground for love defined as 'he laid down his life for us.' John reads self-giving death as the measure of love. The Servant's poured-out life is the template.

echoes.text: Whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor, he will also cry out, but shall not be heard.
echoes.note: Whoever shuts his ears to the cry of the poor will himself cry and not be heard, linking refusal of compassion to severed relationship with God. This grounds John's rhetorical 'how does the love of God remain in him?' A close wisdom parallel to closing the heart against the needy.

echoes.text: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]
echoes.note: Tobit's counsel to give alms from one's goods, not turning the face from any poor person, parallels the test of love by sharing the world's goods with a brother in need. This deuterocanonical almsgiving ethic mirrors John's 'in deed and truth.' A strong thematic echo of practical charity.

echoes.text: My son, deprive not the poor of his living, And make not the needy eyes to wait long. Make not a hungry soul sorrowful; Neither provoke a man in his distress. To a heart that is provoked add not more trouble; And defer not to give to him that is in need. Reject not a suppliant in his affliction; And turn not away your face from a poor man. Turn not away your eye from one that asks of you, And give none occasion to a man to curse you:
echoes.note: Sirach warns against defrauding the poor, turning away the needy, or averting the eye from one in want. This closely matches the one who 'sees his brother in need' yet closes his heart. A deuterocanonical parallel to loving in deed not word.

echoes.text: Don’t withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in the power of your hand to do it. Don’t say to your neighbor, “Go, and come again; tomorrow I will give it to you,” when you have it by you.
echoes.note: 'Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due when it is in your power to do it' parallels John's rebuke of the one who has goods yet withholds them. The duty to act on present means matches 'has the world's goods.' Faint sapiential resonance.

echoes.text: Yahweh, you have searched me, and you know me. You know my sitting down and my rising up. You perceive my thoughts from afar. You search out my path and my lying down, and are acquainted with all my ways. For there is not a word on my tongue, but, behold, Yahweh, you know it altogether.
echoes.note: God searches and knows the heart, discerning thoughts and words before they are spoken, the ground of 'God is greater than our heart, and knows all things.' John reassures the self-condemning conscience by appeal to this divine omniscience. The all-knowing God who weighs the heart is the precise reference.

echoes.text: then hear in heaven, your dwelling place, and forgive, and do, and render to every man according to all his ways, whose heart you know; (for you, even you only, know the hearts of all the children of men;)
echoes.note: Solomon prays that God, who 'alone knows the hearts of all the children of men,' will render to each accordingly. This explicit claim that God alone knows every heart underlies 'God... knows all things.' The heart-knowing God before whom we are persuaded is drawn from this temple prayer.

echoes.text: Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but Yahweh weighs the hearts.
echoes.note: A person's ways seem right to himself, but the LORD weighs the heart, juxtaposing human self-judgment with divine assessment. This parallels the contrast between our condemning heart and the God who is greater and knows all. A wisdom echo of the heart-weighing motif.

echoes.text: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.
echoes.note: 'I the LORD search the heart and test the mind, to give every man according to his ways,' a key heart-searching text. It reinforces John's appeal to the God who knows all things beyond our heart's verdict. Congruent with the omniscience theme.

echoes.text: It shall be righteousness to us, if we observe to do all this commandment before Yahweh our God, as he has commanded us.”
echoes.note: Keeping the commandments before the LORD is reckoned as righteousness, undergirding confidence before God grounded in 'we keep his commandments.' John's boldness toward God rests on obedience as in this Deuteronomic logic. Faint background.

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself' is the OT command standing behind John's commandment that 'we should... love one another.' John joins this love-command to belief in the Son as the single commandment. The mutual-love mandate is rooted in the Holiness Code.

echoes.text: I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: God promises to put his Spirit within his people and cause them to keep his statutes, directly behind 'by the Spirit which he gave us' as the proof of indwelling and obedience. John's pairing of the given Spirit with commandment-keeping mirrors this new-covenant gift. The indwelling Spirit enabling obedience is the source idea.

echoes.text: You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
echoes.note: The Shema's command to love God and the broader keeping of his commandments frames 'we keep his commandments' and abiding obedience. John's interiorized obedience and indwelling echo the covenant heart-love. A thematic resonance with keeping the commandments.

echoes.text: I will put my Spirit in you, and you shall live, and I will place you in your own land: and you shall know that I, Yahweh, have spoken it and performed it, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'I will put my Spirit in you, and you shall live,' the promise of the indwelling life-giving Spirit. This reinforces 'we know that he remains in us, by the Spirit which he gave us.' A strong new-covenant Spirit parallel.

echoes.text: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:
echoes.note: The new covenant writes the law on the heart so the people keep it from within, undergirding the union of commandment-keeping and mutual indwelling ('he remains in us'). John's interior obedience and abiding reflect this new-covenant interiority. A strong conceptual parallel to keeping his commandments.

echoes.text: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions. And also on the servants and on the handmaids in those days, I will pour out my Spirit.
echoes.note: God's promise to pour out his Spirit on all flesh stands in the background of the Spirit given to the community as the sign of God's abiding. Faint, but part of the prophetic Spirit-gift matrix John draws on. Contested as a specific source.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: For thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I myself, even I, will search for my sheep, and will seek them out. As a shepherd seeks out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep that are scattered abroad, so will I seek out my sheep; and I will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day. I will bring them out from the peoples, and gather them from the countries, and will bring them into their own land; and I […]
echoes.note: The LORD himself seeks, gathers, and feeds the scattered sheep, rescuing them from where they were scattered in the day of clouds. Jesus as the good shepherd who knows his own enacts the LORD's own pastoral self-commitment, making the divine claim of Ezekiel 34 the load-bearing subtext.

echoes.text: I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd. I, Yahweh, will be their God, and my servant David prince among them; I, Yahweh, have spoken it.
echoes.note: 'I will set up one shepherd over them, my servant David... and I the LORD will be their God.' This is the source of the singular good shepherd and converges with v.16's 'one flock, one shepherd.' High volume and exact thematic match to the Davidic-messianic single shepherd.

echoes.text: My servant David shall be king over them; and they all shall have one shepherd: they shall also walk in my ordinances, and observe my statutes, and do them.
echoes.note: 'David my servant shall be king over them; and they all shall have one shepherd' is the closest verbal antecedent to 'one flock, one shepherd' (v.16). Recurs with Ezek 34:23 and reinforces the reunification of a divided flock under one Davidic shepherd.

echoes.text: He will feed his flock like a shepherd. He will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom. He will gently lead those who have their young.
echoes.note: 'He will feed his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arm' supplies the tender LORD-as-shepherd image behind the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep. Coherent with John's identification of Jesus with the LORD's own shepherding care.

echoes.text: Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul. He guides me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake. Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me. Your rod and your staff, they comfort me.
echoes.note: 'The LORD is my shepherd... though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death.' The good shepherd who lays down his life and faces the wolf evokes the shepherd who protects through death's shadow. Strong cultural availability, though the laying-down-of-life motif goes beyond Psalm 23.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to me, “Take for yourself yet again the equipment of a foolish shepherd. For, behold, I will raise up a shepherd in the land, who will not visit those who are cut off, neither will seek those who are scattered, nor heal that which is broken, nor feed that which is sound; but he will eat the flesh of the fat sheep, and will tear their hoofs in pieces. Woe to the worthless shepherd who leaves the flock! The sword will be on his arm, and on his […]
echoes.note: The 'worthless shepherd' who deserts the flock, does not care for the perishing, and abandons them to be devoured is the negative counterpart to John's hired hand who flees the wolf and does not care for the sheep. Verbal and thematic coherence in the abandonment/devouring imagery.

echoes.text: They were scattered, because there was no shepherd; and they became food to all the animals of the field, and were scattered. My sheep wandered through all the mountains, and on every high hill: yes, my sheep were scattered on all the surface of the earth; and there was no one who searched or sought.
echoes.note: Without a shepherd the flock 'became food for all the beasts of the field, and were scattered.' The wolf that snatches and scatters the sheep (v.12) replays Ezekiel's scattering and devouring of the unshepherded flock.

echoes.text: The Lord Yahweh, who gathers the outcasts of Israel, says, “Yet will I gather others to him, besides his own who are gathered.”
echoes.note: 'The Lord GOD, who gathers the outcasts of Israel, says, Yet others will I gather besides his own that are gathered.' This is the strongest antecedent for the 'other sheep... not of this fold' whom the shepherd must also bring (v.16), grounding the Gentile ingathering.

echoes.text: I will surely assemble, Jacob, all of you; I will surely gather the remnant of Israel; I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as a flock in the midst of their pasture; they will swarm with people.
echoes.note: 'I will surely gather all of you, Jacob... I will put them together like the sheep of Bozrah... they will swarm with people.' Supplies the regathering-into-one-flock image behind the 'one flock' formed from other sheep. Coherent but competes with Ezekiel/Isaiah gathering texts.

echoes.text: He shall stand, and shall shepherd in the strength of Yahweh, in the majesty of the name of Yahweh his God: and they will live, for then he will be great to the ends of the earth.
echoes.note: 'He shall stand and shepherd his flock in the strength of the LORD' offers the messianic ruler-as-shepherd whose flock dwells securely 'to the ends of the earth,' faintly behind the universal one-flock vision. Lower volume than the Ezekiel cluster.

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all. He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is mute, so he didn’t open his mouth. He was taken away by oppression and judgment; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living and […]
echoes.note: 'All we like sheep have gone astray... the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all,' and the servant who 'poured out his soul to death.' The shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep may fuse the suffering servant with the shepherd. Contested and faint in John, which rarely cites Isaiah 53 explicitly.

lines: The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want.
He leads us beside still waters.
We have wandered through the valley of shadow.
But you are with us; we fear no evil.
The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
Come, let us worship; he knows us by name.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Come and lie down in the green grass, you who are tired of running, and let the Shepherd lead you to still water.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
He calls each of us by name, and we know his voice, the way sheep know the one who feeds them.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
He does not run when the wolf comes; he is no hired hand; he lays down his life for the sheep.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
And though we walk through the darkest valley, his rod and staff are with us, and his table is already set.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
